# Zephaniah 3: verse-by-verse research notes

**What I couldn't find.** I ran out of searches before I could check the Catholic and Orthodox sites (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org), bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching about this chapter. Those sections are left out. Verses 6, 10, 18 and 19 have only thin notes.

**Where Protestant teachers really differ.** The split is about end times more than denomination. Some read vv. 9–20 as a promise about a future thousand-year reign of Christ on earth (the "millennium"): Guzik at Enduring Word, GotQuestions, Chuck Smith (whom StudyLight labels Calvary Chapel / Dispensationalism) and Ironside. Others read it as fulfilled in the return from exile, the gospel and the church: Matthew Henry, Barnes, Gill (labelled Baptist / Calvinism) and Coffman (labelled Restoration Movement / Arminianism).

**Background.** Precept Austin dates the book to King Josiah's reign. It reproduces Walter Kaiser's outline along with outlines by MacDonald and Wiersbe. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah-3-commentary) The Pulpit Commentary thinks it must have been written before the great reformation. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/3-3.htm)

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik says that after chapter 2 we might expect this city to be Nineveh. But the mention of her prophets, priests, sanctuary and law shows it is Jerusalem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zephaniah-3/
- Matthew Henry notes other readings of "filthy": "infamous," or the margin's "gluttonous" city. He adds that no place had such righteous laws, yet none was governed more unrighteously. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zep/Zep_003.cfm

**v. 2**
- Guzik sees the four "she has not" lines as the root of Jerusalem's sin. He treats the last one, not drawing near, as the worst offense. On "correction," he says correction did come, but she did not receive it as from the LORD. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zephaniah-3/
- Precept Austin says that by depending on human alliances and idols, Judah showed a heart turned away from God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah-3-commentary
- Matthew Henry says her confidence was in alliances with the nations more than in her covenant with God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zep/Zep_003.cfm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) points out the irony: God was specially near to her, yet she estranged herself from Him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Zep/Zep_003.cfm

**v. 3**
- Pulpit Commentary: the princes ought to protect the people but tear them in pieces. The judges are themselves most cruel and rapacious. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/3-3.htm
- Calvin: the judges are like wolves that become furious in the evening after finding nothing all day. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zephaniah/3-3.html
- Coffman: the judges are worse than wolves. A wolf keeps some of its kill for the next day, but the false judges made a clean end of their victims. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zephaniah/3-3.html
- Gill also applies the verse to the Sanhedrin that crucified the Lord of glory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/3-3.htm
- The phrase about the morning is debated. The Cambridge Bible gives two readings: wolves that had no prey in the morning and so were ferocious in the evening, or wolves that leave nothing till morning. It admits the second is somewhat conjectural. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/3-3.htm
- BibleHub's study notes add that God told Israel to leave leftovers for the needy, yet these leaders left "nothing." https://biblehub.com/zephaniah/3-3.htm

**v. 4**
- Precept Austin: the priests should have guarded the temple's holiness. Instead, they blurred the line between holy and profane. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah-3-commentary
- Keil and Delitzsch explain "do violence to the law" as treating the holy as profane and perverting the law's precepts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/zephaniah/3.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary's homiletics section calls the prophets trifling and insincere, so their words could not be relied on. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zephaniah-3.html

**v. 5**
- Guzik: God's righteousness in the city's midst made His people's unrighteousness even more criminal and tragic. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zephaniah-3/
- Ironside, who reads the chapter as being about the millennium, applies "morning by morning" to the coming kingdom, when morning by morning the wicked will be cut off. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/zephaniah-3.html

**vv. 6–7**
- Guzik: God's judgments on nearby nations should have warned Judah. Instead they gave themselves to ungodliness all the more. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zephaniah-3/
- Matthew Henry: had they taken the warning, the past would have been pardoned and their peace lengthened. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zep/Zep_003.cfm

**v. 8**
- The Gospel Coalition's structure note: the prophet commands them to wait for the Lord (3:8) to enjoy satisfying salvation. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/zephaniah/
- Precept Austin on the word "wait": in its fullest sense it means faithful perseverance by those who trust God's promises. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah-3-commentary
- JFB says the nations are gathered against Jerusalem (Zec 14:2), where God pours out His anger on them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Zep/Zep_003.cfm
- Translation note: BSB has "rise to testify," but ESV has "rise up to seize the prey." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/zephaniah/3-9.html Keil takes the Hebrew as "for prey." He also argues that God's "rising up" cannot refer to the Messiah's coming or Christ's resurrection, as the older writer Cocceius thought. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/zephaniah/3.htm

**v. 9** (a verse where readers divide)
- Calvin (Reformed): the pure lip means God's drawing comes first. God cannot be rightly called on until He draws us, for our lips are impure. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zephaniah/3-9.html
- Keil, quoted by Constable, says "lip" is not about language as such: pure lips presuppose a purified heart. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zephaniah/3-9.html
- Reading 1, Pentecost: Barnes says God gave back one pure language at Pentecost when the Spirit came in fiery tongues. JFB calls Pentecost an earnest of the removal of this penalty, meaning the Babel judgment. It adds that full fulfilment is yet future, connected with the restoration of the Jews. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/3-9.htm and https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Zep/Zep_003.cfm
- Coffman agrees: not better Hebrew, but hearts conformed to God's will. He calls Pentecost a token fulfillment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/zephaniah-3.html
- Reading 2, the millennium: Guzik says most scholars see this fulfilled in the Millennium, and that many expect a common language, perhaps Hebrew. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zephaniah-3/ Chuck Smith likewise says the day is coming when we'll speak a pure language again. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zephaniah/3-9.html
- Matthew Henry applies the verse to Christian unity: "Purity is the way to unity." He also links "shoulder to shoulder" to oxen pulling evenly in a yoke. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zep/Zep_003.cfm
- Gill reads the "pure language" as the gospel itself, a language of love, grace, and mercy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/3-9.htm

**v. 10**
- Cambridge Bible: vv. 9–10 speak of the nations, vv. 11–13 of Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/3-9.htm
- Precept Austin's word study on "scattered" says the God who scatters will one day gather them again. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah-3-commentary

**v. 11**
- Guzik: in the millennium Israel will be powerful but not haughty, knowing her standing is all of grace. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zephaniah-3/
- Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary: the Lord leaves men nothing to glory in but the Lord Jesus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/3-9.htm

**v. 12**
- Matthew Henry reads the humble people as the poor in spirit and as a remnant according to the election of grace. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zep/Zep_003.cfm
- Precept Austin cross-references the remnant to Isaiah 10, Micah 4:7 and Romans 11:4–7. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah-3-commentary

**v. 13**
- Matthew Henry: the promise goes beyond avoiding outright lies; not even the least equivocation will be found. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zep/Zep_003.cfm
- Guzik: "feed and lie down" pictures peace and prosperity in the millennial era. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zephaniah-3/

**v. 14**
- Barnes quotes Rupert, a medieval writer, who reads the threefold call to joy through the Trinity: sing to the Father, shout to the Son, rejoice in the Holy Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/zephaniah/3-14.html
- Adam Clarke sees not only return from captivity but their conversion to God through Christ. (same URL)

**v. 15**
- Precept Austin: the heart of the verse is God's presence. It sees the Messiah filling the gap left by removed judgment as the true King reigning in Jerusalem. It also says there will come a day when Jehovah will cease punishing His rebellious people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah-3-commentary

**v. 16**
- Guzik draws two responses. We should not fear, and we should not let our hands be weak, because we want to be for Him with all our energy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zephaniah-3/

**v. 17** (the chapter's best-known verse)
- Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik, says God did not sing when he made the world, but rejoices over the salvation of His redeemed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zephaniah-3/
- Piper (Baptist, Desiring God), via Precept Austin: the verse applies to believing Jews and to Gentiles who are heirs of the promise through faith in Christ. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah_317_commentary
- Keith Mathison (Reformed, Tabletalk), via the same page: this is not Aristotle's "Unmoved Mover." (same URL)
- Gill gives the verse a Christ-centred reading: a pleonasm of joy in Christ's heart towards his people, meaning more joy than words can hold. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/3-17.htm
- Lutheran (1517.org): the people's earlier loud cries of sadness are overcome by the louder singing of God. https://www.1517.org/articles/how-god-loves-us-the-sound-of-salvation-zephaniah-317
- The millennial reading: GotQuestions says Zephaniah speaks of the future millennial kingdom. It also cautions that whether God Himself sings is not made clear, since the Hebrew can mean a shout of joy. https://www.gotquestions.org/rejoice-with-singing.html
- Translation note on "quiet you with His love." Other versions have "be silent in his love" or "renew you" (NET), and the Amplified adds "[making no mention of your past sins]". https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rsv/zephaniah/3-17.html Precept Austin explains the Hebrew word as to be silent, still, or at rest. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah-3-commentary One older commentator on BibleHub's page compares it to God resting in silent satisfaction after creation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/3-17.htm

**v. 18**
- Matthew Henry: those who grieve mourn the ruined sanctuary more than the ruined city. It is for those sacred solemn assemblies that they are sorrowful. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zep/Zep_003.cfm
- Keil discusses the difficult grammar of this verse; for example, scholars dispute what the suffix refers to. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/zephaniah/3.htm

**v. 19**
- Guzik: God promises to encourage the discouraged, defeat enemies, heal the lame, and gather the scattered. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zephaniah-3/

**v. 20**
- Matthew Henry: they will see God's hand clearly and say, "This is the Lord's doing." He extends the promise to the universal church on the great day. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zep/Zep_003.cfm
- The Gospel Coalition: those who seek and wait for God are the ones he will exalt "among all the peoples of the earth." https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/zephaniah/
- Precept Austin calls "says the LORD" a solemn vow by God to do as He has promised. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah-3-commentary
